title: Ferromagnetism
short_intro: Ferromagnetism is a phenomenon where certain materials, such as iron, cobalt, and nickel, exhibit strong permanent magnetization below a specific characteristic temperature known as the Curie temperature. This behavior arises from the strong quantum mechanical exchange coupling between adjacent atomic magnetic dipole moments, aligning them parallel to each other within microscopic regions called domains.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Qualitative understanding of ferromagnetic substances, domain theory, Curie temperature, hysteresis loop, and basic retentivity and coercivity concepts.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Quantitative treatment of Weiss molecular field theory, Curie-Weiss law for susceptibility, magnetic domain wall energy, and energy losses in hysteresis cycles.

prerequisites: Atomic magnetic dipole moments and Bohr magneton
Magnetic intensity (H), magnetic induction (B), and magnetization (M)

concept_notes.heading: Origin of Ferromagnetism and Exchange Interaction
bullets: Ferromagnetism originates from the quantum mechanical exchange interaction, electrostatic in origin, which couples adjacent electron spins.
The exchange energy favors parallel alignment of spins when the exchange integral is positive, overcoming thermal agitation at low temperatures.
It leads to spontaneous magnetization within small regions termed magnetic domains even in the absence of an external magnetic field.

concept_notes.heading: Domain Theory of Ferromagnetism
bullets: A macroscopic ferromagnetic sample is divided into numerous microscopic regions called domains, each uniformly magnetized to saturation.
In an unmagnetized state, the net magnetic moment of the bulk material is zero due to the random orientations of the individual domain magnetic moments.
Application of an external magnetic field causes domain growth through boundary displacement and subsequent domain rotation toward the field direction.

concept_notes.heading: Curie-Weiss Law and Temperature Dependence
bullets: Above a critical temperature called the Curie temperature (T<sub>C</sub>), a ferromagnetic material transitions into a paramagnetic state.
The magnetic susceptibility (χ) above T<sub>C</sub> follows the Curie-Weiss law given by χ = C / (T - T<sub>C</sub>), where C is the Curie constant.
Below T<sub>C</sub>, the thermal energy is insufficient to overcome the internal exchange field, preserving spontaneous alignment.

concept_notes.heading: Hysteresis and Magnetic Properties
bullets: Hysteresis is the lag of magnetic induction (B) behind the magnetizing field (H) during a complete cycle of magnetization and demagnetization.
Retentivity (or remanence) is the residual magnetic induction retained by the material when the external field H is reduced to zero.
Coercivity is the magnitude of the reverse magnetizing field required to reduce the residual magnetic induction to zero.

derivations.title: Weiss Molecular Field Theory and Curie-Weiss Law
derivations.conditions: Applied to ferromagnetic materials in the paramagnetic region (T > T_C)
steps: Assume an internal molecular field B<sub>m</sub> proportional to the magnetization M, given by B<sub>m</sub> = λM, where λ is the Weiss molecular field constant.
The total effective magnetic field acting on the atomic dipoles is B<sub>eff</sub> = B + B<sub>m</sub> = B + λM, where B is the applied external field.
Using the standard paramagnetic susceptibility formula based on Langevin's theory, M = (C' / T) B<sub>eff</sub>, substitute B<sub>eff</sub> to get M = (C' / T)(B + λM).
Express B / μ<sub>0</sub> as H and use M = χH. Rearrange the equation to solve for magnetic susceptibility χ.

derivations.title: Energy Dissipation per Unit Volume per Hysteresis Cycle
derivations.conditions: Quasi-static cyclic magnetization of a ferromagnetic core
steps: The work done per unit volume in changing the magnetization by dM in an external field H is dW = H dB.
Since B = \mu_0 (H + M), the infinitesimal work is dW = \mu_0 H dH + \mu_0 H dM.
Integrating over a complete closed hysteresis cycle, the term involving H dH vanishes because the initial and final states are identical.
The net work done, which appears entirely as thermal energy dissipated per unit volume per cycle, equals the area enclosed by the B-H (or M-H) hysteresis loop.
derivations.result: W = \oint H \, dB = \text{Area of the B-H loop}

graphs_and_experiments.title: B-H Hysteresis Loop
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A closed loop plotting Magnetic Induction (B) on the y-axis against Magnetic Intensity (H) on the x-axis, showing saturation, retentivity (B<sub>r</sub>), and coercivity (H<sub>c</sub>).
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The non-linear response and loop area quantify the energy dissipated per cycle. Retentivity indicates memory retention; coercivity indicates resistance to demagnetization.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Direct identification questions on soft and hard magnetic materials based on loop geometry (narrow vs. wide).

graphs_and_experiments.title: Susceptibility vs. Temperature (Curie-Weiss Law)
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A plot of inverse magnetic susceptibility (1/χ) versus temperature (T), showing a linear increase above T<sub>C</sub> that extrapolates to intercept the temperature axis at T = T<sub>C</sub>.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrates the phase transition from ferromagnetism to paramagnetism at the Curie point.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Numerical and conceptual problems on Curie constant calculation and temperature scaling.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Rowland Ring Experiment
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A toroidal ferromagnetic ring wound uniformly with a primary magnetizing coil and a secondary search coil connected to a ballistic galvanometer.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Allows experimental determination of the B-H curve and hysteresis loops for a given ferromagnetic specimen.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Conceptual questions on experimental setup parameters and flux linkage measurement.

solved_numericals.question: A ferromagnetic material has a relative permeability of 1000. Calculate its magnetic susceptibility.
solution_steps: Recall the relation between relative permeability (μ<sub>r</sub>) and magnetic susceptibility (χ): μ<sub>r</sub> = 1 + χ.

solved_numericals.question: The magnetic susceptibility of a ferromagnetic material is 4.0 × 10<sup>-3</sup> at a temperature of 400 K. If its Curie temperature is 300 K, find the susceptibility at 500 K.
solution_steps: According to the Curie-Weiss law, χ = C / (T - T<sub>C</sub>), which implies χ(T - T<sub>C</sub>) = C (a constant).

Set up the ratio for two temperatures T<sub>1</sub> = 400 K and T<sub>2</sub> = 500 K with T<sub>C</sub> = 300 K: χ<sub>1</sub>(T<sub>1</sub> - T<sub>C</sub>) = χ<sub>2</sub>(T<sub>2</sub> - T<sub>C</sub>).

solved_numericals.question: Calculate the energy dissipated per unit volume per cycle for a hysteresis loop whose area is equivalent to 500 J/m<sup>3</sup>.
solution_steps: Recall that the energy loss per unit volume per cycle is numerically equal to the area of the B-H (or μ<sub>0</sub>H-M) hysteresis loop.
Given the loop area directly represents the work done per unit volume: W = ∮ H dB = 500 J/m<sup>3</sup>.

assumptions_and_limitations: Weiss molecular field theory assumes a uniform effective internal field acting on every atomic dipole, which is an oversimplification of quantum mechanical exchange interactions.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Ferromagnetic materials retain permanent magnetism indefinitely without any external influence.
common_misconceptions.correct: Permanent magnetism depends on high coercivity and retentivity; mechanical shock, heating above T<sub>C</sub>, or stray reverse fields can demagnetize them.
common_misconceptions.why: Thermal agitation and stray magnetic fields can disrupt domain alignment over time if coercivity is low.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Magnetic susceptibility of a ferromagnet is constant like that of a paramagnet.
common_misconceptions.correct: Susceptibility in ferromagnets is highly non-linear, field-dependent, and varies strongly with temperature according to the Curie-Weiss law above T<sub>C</sub>.
common_misconceptions.why: Ferromagnetism involves cooperative domain phenomena rather than independent atomic dipole responses.

quick_revision: Ferromagnetism arises from quantum exchange coupling aligning atomic dipoles parallel within domains.
Above the Curie temperature (T<sub>C</sub>), a ferromagnet becomes paramagnetic obeying χ = C / (T - T<sub>C</sub>).
Area of the B-H hysteresis loop represents thermal energy loss per unit volume per cycle.
Soft magnetic materials have narrow loops (low coercivity, high permeability), while hard magnetic materials have wide loops (high coercivity, high retentivity).
